conflict_topics: Who will complete Agent D's section for the client pitch (coverage of work / deadline responsibility)
dialogue_quality_notes: Turns are natural and role-appropriate: condolence followed by practical problem-solving.
Refusals include concrete reasons ('covering for Amir', 'my section is behind', 'don't know how to do her analysis'), which grounds the negotiation.
Resolution is achieved by a concrete promise from the person responsible rather than by pressure on other team members.
Some repeated brief 'Thanks.' lines occur but do not impede clarity.
evaluation.final_reason: Agent D committed to finish their section from home and the team accepted that plan. Key lines: Agent D: 'I can work from home. I'll finish my section. You don't need to cover for me.' Agent A (accepting): 'Okay, Agent D. Thank you. We are counting on you. Keep us updated...' This mutual acceptance ended the coverage conflict.
position_change_notes: Agent D moved from announcing a personal need to offering and reaffirming a commitment to finish the section ('I can work from home... I will manage it').
Agent A shifted from proposing redistribution of D's work to accepting D's commitment and relying on it ('We are counting on you').
Agent B and Agent C retained their initial refusals to take on additional work, with reasons given; they did not change position.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A offers condolences and asks if Agent D needs to go be with family; Agent D confirms. No incompatible claims or demands expressed.

Agent A proposes the team cover Agent D's section: '...that means we need to cover Agent D's section. Let's look at what's left and divide it between the three of us.' Agent B refuses: 'I can't. I'm already covering for Amir. I've worked late every night this week.' Clear, unresolved disagreement about who will cover the work.

Agent A asks Agent C to split the remaining work with A; Agent C refuses and gives reasons: 'I can't... My section is behind already, and I don't know how to do her analysis work.' The coverage problem persists and another team member declines, increasing strain on the proposal.

Agent D offers to work from home and finish the section: 'I can work from home. I'll finish my section. You don't need to cover for me.' Agent A asks 'are you sure?' — the offer reduces the active incompatibility but others have not yet explicitly accepted the new plan.

Agent D reaffirms the plan: 'Yes. I need to be with my family, and the work needs to get done. I will manage it.' This strengthens D's promise but the team has not yet explicitly completed acceptance, so a small amount of uncertainty remains.

Agent A accepts D's commitment and places reliance on it: 'Okay, Agent D. Thank you. We are counting on you. Keep us updated...' Agent D: 'I will.' The practical incompatibility (who will complete the section) is affirmatively settled by D's promise and A's acceptance.

substantive_insights: Capacity constraints and skill mismatch drove refusals: B cited workload, C cited being behind and lacking analysis skills.
The clearest path to resolving a last-minute gap was the owner (Agent D) taking responsibility rather than redistributing tasks.
Concrete, actionable commitments (who will do what) resolved the practical incompatibility; expressions of sympathy alone did not.
